name: The Court of Yes and No

exhibits.title: The Court of Yes and No
exhibits.text:
A lattice of glowing orbs hangs in the air — the same N×N matrix from the Paired Lanterns, one orb for every image-caption pair, the true pairs burning along the diagonal. But this lattice performs two verdicts, one after the other, and the whole lesson of SigLIP is the difference between them.

FIRST, THE OLD WAY. A luminous bracket sweeps down a single row, and as it passes, the orbs in that row COMPETE — brighten one and the others must dim, all of them bound together, their glows summing to a fixed whole. This is the softmax of CLIP: a relative contest, 'which of these N is the best match?', every orb's fate coupled to its neighbours across the entire row.

THEN, THE NEW WAY. The bracket vanishes. Every orb in the lattice settles on its own, at the same instant, each one answering a single private question — 'do THESE two match? yes or no?' — and glowing to its own steady brightness with no glance at any other. No competition, no shared budget, no bracket sweeping through. This is the sigmoid of SigLIP: an ABSOLUTE, per-cell judgment. Watch the two modes alternate, and you have watched the one change that separates CLIP from SigLIP — not a new eye, not a new matrix, only a new way of passing judgment on each cell.

exhibits.title: One Change: Sigmoid, Not Softmax
exhibits.text:
SigLIP keeps everything about CLIP — same two encoders, same shared space, same N×N similarity matrix — and changes exactly ONE thing: the loss.

  CLIP:   for image i, softmax over all N captions → 'which caption is correct?'  (RELATIVE)
  SigLIP: for EACH pair (i,j) on its own          → 'do these two match? yes/no'  (ABSOLUTE)

The matrix is still computed in full, but now every cell carries its OWN binary label — 1 on the diagonal (a true pair), 0 everywhere else — and its own independent loss:

           cap1  cap2  cap3  cap4
    img1 [  1     0     0     0  ]
    img2 [  0     1     0     0  ]
    img3 [  0     0     1     0  ]
    img4 [  0     0     0     1  ]

Each cell: sigmoid(similarity) → binary cross-entropy against its 0/1 label. That is the whole change. Softmax asked the cells to compete for a shared pool of probability; sigmoid lets each cell answer alone, yes or no, as if no other cell existed. It is the same independent binary-decision pattern as any yes/no detector — a competition dissolved into a court of private verdicts.

exhibits.title: The Temperature and the Bias
exhibits.text:
Before a similarity becomes a verdict it passes through two learned scalars:

    logit = sim × t + b        (in the worked example, t = 10, b = −5)

t is the TEMPERATURE — a learned scale that sharpens or softens the logits. Cosine similarities live in a cramped [−1, 1]; multiplying by t stretches them into a range where sigmoid can commit to confident yeses and noes.

b is the BIAS — a learned offset, and it is NEGATIVE on purpose. In an N×N matrix only the N diagonal cells are positives; the other N²−N are negatives. With N=3 that is 3 yeses against 6 noes; at real batch sizes the imbalance is far more lopsided. A negative bias shifts every cell's DEFAULT verdict toward 'no match', so the model does not have to fight the flood of negatives from scratch — it starts out expecting 'no' and learns which rare cells deserve a 'yes'. Both t and b are trained right alongside the encoder weights.

exhibits.title: Decoupled: No All-Gather, Small Batches
exhibits.text:
Because each cell's loss is computed completely on its own — no cell needs any other cell's value — the batch is no longer coupled, and CLIP's whole tax bill disappears:

1. NO BATCH-WIDE NORMALIZATION. There is no softmax denominator spanning the row, so no global sum to compute. Each GPU scores its own chunk of the matrix independently — no all-gather hauling embeddings across the machine.

2. WORKS AT SMALL BATCHES. CLIP needed ~32K to supply enough negatives for its relative contest. SigLIP's binary 'does this pair match?' does not depend on having a huge crowd of rivals, so it trains well at far smaller batch sizes.

3. BETTER SCALING AND EFFICIENCY — cheaper distributed training and better performance per unit of compute.

This is why SigLIP has become the DEFAULT vision encoder in most modern VLMs — PaliGemma, SmolVLM, and many Qwen-VL variants read the world through a SigLIP eye. One change to the loss, and the whole training pipeline gets lighter.

exhibits.spec:

exhibits.caption: The SigLIP loss walked in three panels for one row of an N=3 matrix. Panel one: the cosine similarities (0.82, 0.15, −0.20). Panel two: scale and shift into logits with t=10 and b=−5 (3.20, −3.50, −7.00) — note the negative bias pulling every default toward 'no'. Each cell is computed with no reference to any other — the visible decoupling that lets SigLIP drop the all-gather.

exhibits.title: On SigLIP, and the Full Worked Verdict
exhibits.text:
SigLIP — SIGMOID INSTEAD OF SOFTMAX

SigLIP changes ONE thing about CLIP: the loss. Same architecture, same shared space, same N×N matrix — but every pair becomes an INDEPENDENT binary classification.

    CLIP:   for image i, softmax over all N captions → 'which caption is correct?'  (relative)
    SigLIP: for each pair (i,j) independently        → 'do these two match? yes/no'  (absolute)

Each cell of the matrix gets its own binary label — 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere — and its own loss: sigmoid(similarity) → binary cross-entropy against that 0/1 label. It is the same BCE-with-logits pattern as any independent yes/no decision — not a competition.

THE WORKED EXAMPLE (N = 3).

Step 1 — the similarity matrix (L2-normalized embeddings, cosine sim in [−1, 1]):

           cap1    cap2    cap3
    img1 [ 0.82   0.15   −0.20 ]
    img2 [ 0.10   0.75    0.05 ]
    img3 [−0.05   0.22    0.68 ]

Step 2 — scale by learned temperature t and add learned bias b:

    logit = sim × t + b        (t = 10, b = −5)

    img1-cap1:  0.82 × 10 − 5  =  3.20
    img1-cap2:  0.15 × 10 − 5  = −3.50
    img1-cap3: −0.20 × 10 − 5  = −7.00

b is negative because most pairs are negatives — only 3 positives out of 9 cells — so the default verdict is shifted toward 'no match', handling the imbalance.

Step 3 — sigmoid → probability, then binary cross-entropy:

    img1-cap1:  sigmoid(3.20)  = 0.961   label=1 → −log(0.961)     = 0.040
    img1-cap2:  sigmoid(−3.50) = 0.029   label=0 → −log(1 − 0.029) = 0.030
    img1-cap3:  sigmoid(−7.00) = 0.001   label=0 → −log(1 − 0.001) = 0.001

Standard BCE: −[y·log(p) + (1−y)·log(1−p)]. When y=1 it is −log(p); when y=0 it is −log(1−p).

Step 4 — average over all N² cells.

KEY OBSERVATION: each cell was computed COMPLETELY INDEPENDENTLY — no cell needed any other cell's value. That is the decoupling. Contrast CLIP, where computing img1's loss requires the softmax denominator summing across the whole row.

TRAINABLE QUANTITIES IN PLAY:
    Encoder weights → shape the embeddings → shape the similarities.
    t (temperature) → learned scalar, sharpens or softens the logits.
    b (bias)        → learned scalar, offsets the positive/negative imbalance.

THE PAYOFF. No batch-wide normalization → no all-gather; each GPU scores its own chunk. Works well at small batch sizes — the binary objective does not depend on having many negatives the way CLIP's ~32K does. Better scaling and efficiency overall. This is why SigLIP is the default vision encoder in most modern VLMs (PaliGemma, SmolVLM, Qwen-VL variants). If you want the raw mathematics of relative-versus-absolute judgment — softmax's coupling against sigmoid's independence, stripped of all vision talk — follow the portal down to the Two Judgments in the foundations below.
